question: When a supervised image classifier is deeper or wider than its task requires, do early layers finish constructing linearly separable features while later layers mainly compress them, and how does that layerwise transition affect transfer and continual learning?

key_findings.claim: Every tested small-image configuration contains a late segment with saturated in-distribution probes and falling representation rank, but its length is definition-dependent.
key_findings.evidence: The authors call the first layer reaching 95% or 98% of final linear-probe accuracy the tunnel boundary. Table 1 places it at layers 4-5 of a 13-layer MLP, 7-8 of VGG-19, and 17-30 of ResNet-34 depending on dataset and threshold. Switching the threshold by architecture and counting conventions makes the exact length a diagnostic choice rather than a natural discontinuity.

key_findings.claim: The late layers compress source-task representations toward class-scale rank while preserving almost all source linear separability.
key_findings.evidence: For MLPs and VGGs on CIFAR-10, the numerical rank estimated at a relative singular-value threshold falls near ten as probes plateau. VGG inter-class distances rise, within-class variance falls, UMAP clusters tighten, and CKA shows a block of similar late representations. ResNet ranks are higher and non-monotone, including a skip-linked spike near layer 29.

key_findings.claim: The rank transition appears during the first updates and persists, although late-layer parameters are not functionally inert.
key_findings.evidence: In VGG-19, deep-layer rank collapses during roughly the first 75 updates and stays low; late weights also change less after early training. Resetting those weights to their pre-optimization values nevertheless severely harms performance, showing that small parameter movement and saturated probes do not mean the tunnel can simply be replaced by its initialization.

key_findings.claim: Target-task linear-probe accuracy usually peaks near the tunnel entrance and then falls with numerical rank.
key_findings.evidence: Backbones trained on CIFAR-10 are probed using labels from held-out CIFAR-100 classes and several other datasets; MLP, VGG, ResNet, and appendix curves generally decline through the tunnel, with a ResNet skip-stage spike and weaker decline for semantically overlapping STL-10. This measures supervised transfer of frozen features, not unlabeled OOD detection or zero-shot generalization, and the depth correlation alone does not establish compression as the cause.

key_findings.claim: Excess capacity lengthens the measured tunnel, while class count is a stronger predictor than sample count in the selected datasets.
key_findings.evidence: Deeper MLPs and VGGs start their tunnel at nearly the same layer, so added layers enlarge the tail; width usually moves the boundary earlier, though ResNet-34 breaks the monotone width trend. CIFAR-10 and three-times-larger CINIC-10 yield similar VGG boundaries, whereas more CIFAR-100 classes shorten tunnels. Dataset, resolution, label granularity, and class count remain confounded outside these controlled subsets.

key_findings.claim: A late tunnel can be swapped across equal-cardinality split-CIFAR-10 tasks with little additional accuracy change, but this task-agnostic claim fails to be unconditional.
key_findings.evidence: Combining first-task and second-task extractors and tunnels changes their respective task accuracies by at most about 1.2 points in the five-versus-five experiment. With three-versus-seven or seven-versus-three tasks, appendix substitution curves depend strongly on which task has more classes, consistent with compression to an effective class count rather than universal task agnosticism.

key_findings.claim: Shallower networks trained from scratch can retain final accuracy and forget less, provided they remain at least as deep as the measured extractor.
key_findings.evidence: In the two-task split-CIFAR-10 VGG experiment, models shortened down to roughly the original extractor boundary match the longer model's task accuracy while showing lower forgetting; performance falls below that depth. Because these are separately trained architectures, the result supports capacity selection but does not validate post-hoc deletion of an already trained tunnel.

key_findings.claim: The evidence is extensive within its regime but cannot support a universal deep-network law.
key_findings.evidence: Roughly 300 final experiments cover MLP, VGG, and ResNet variants, three primary 32-pixel supervised datasets, extra transfer sets, rank/probe/CKA/variance diagnostics, and three-run averages. The paper does not test self-supervised pretraining, transformers, large high-resolution corpora, language, calibration, causal rank interventions, or broad seed uncertainty, and no linked executable artifact appears in the paper or primary records.

method.core_idea: Train image classifiers of varying depth and width, attach a separately optimized linear probe to every hidden layer, define the first near-final probe layer as an extractor/tunnel boundary, and compare layerwise rank, similarity, class geometry, transfer, weight dynamics, and sequential-task substitution around that boundary.
method.mechanism: Supervised cross-entropy first builds features sufficient for source-label separation, after which excess layers increasingly contract within-class variation and discard directions unnecessary for those labels. The resulting low-rank late representation preserves source accuracy but can erase structure useful for a different labeling or distribution.
assumptions: A 95% or 98% probe-accuracy threshold identifies a meaningful layer transition.
A singular value above 0.001 times the maximum is a comparable rank criterion across layers.
Linear probes reveal the task-relevant information available in each representation.
Layerwise rank decline, rather than another depth-varying property, explains transfer decline.
CIFAR/CINIC behavior is representative of sufficiently overparameterized supervised networks.
Network width, depth, and source class count are useful proxies for capacity-task mismatch.

techniques.role: Locates where source and target tasks become linearly separable.
Counts covariance singular values above a layer-relative threshold.
Detects contiguous groups of representationally similar layers.
Separates within-class contraction from between-class expansion.
Tracks weight movement and rank during initial updates and later epochs.
Measures supervised transfer from each frozen source layer.
Combines extractors and tunnels saved after sequential tasks.
Varies depth, width, class count, and sample count proxies.

evaluations.setting: MLP, VGG-16/19, and ResNet-18/34 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10
evaluations.metric: First layer above 95% or 98% of final source linear-probe accuracy and representation rank
evaluations.result: All reported configurations contain a measured tunnel, ranging from roughly 12% to 69% of layers depending on architecture, task, and threshold.
evaluations.baseline: The final network layer's source probe accuracy

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 backbones with CIFAR-100 subsets and multiple external target datasets
evaluations.metric: Layerwise target-label linear-probe accuracy and numerical rank
evaluations.result: Transfer generally peaks near the tunnel entrance and falls through later layers; ResNets show non-monotone stage effects and STL-10 deteriorates least.

evaluations.setting: Depth, width, source-class-count, and CIFAR-10 versus CINIC-10 sweeps
evaluations.metric: Extractor length under the probe threshold
evaluations.result: Extra depth mostly enlarges the tunnel; width usually does so; more source classes generally extend the extractor, while more samples alone do not in the selected comparison.

evaluations.setting: Sequential five/five and unequal split-CIFAR-10 tasks with VGG-19
evaluations.metric: Task accuracy after extractor/tunnel substitution and forgetting versus trained depth
evaluations.result: Equal-class tunnels swap with small effect; unequal-class behavior is asymmetric; shorter-from-scratch models at extractor depth retain accuracy and reduce forgetting.

limitations: Tunnel location is imposed by a 95% or 98% threshold and those thresholds differ across architecture families.
Numerical rank depends on relative singular-value tolerance, feature subsampling, layer width, spatial resolution, and covariance estimation.
Target-label linear probing measures supervised frozen-feature transfer, not zero-shot OOD generalization.
Correlation between rank and target accuracy does not establish rank loss as the causal mechanism.
Primary training uses small 32-pixel classification datasets rather than modern high-resolution or self-supervised pretraining.
Three-run averages do not expose broad seed, split, or hyperparameter uncertainty in most plots.
Continual-learning conclusions come from a two-task split of CIFAR-10 and weaken when task class counts differ.
Short models are retrained from scratch, so the paper does not demonstrate post-hoc tunnel removal from a trained model.
No linked public implementation or exact end-to-end reproduction command was identified.
failure_modes: Changing the probe threshold moves or eliminates the apparent extractor/tunnel split.
A nonlinear or multi-layer target readout recovers information that a late linear probe misses.
Rank falls because spatial dimensions or activation scales change rather than because transferable information is destroyed.
High-resolution, many-class, strongly augmented pretraining does not compress late features.
Residual or transformer pathways produce repeated information expansion and contraction instead of one boundary.
The target task shares source semantics, so late source-specialized features remain highly transferable.
Unequal or hierarchical continual tasks require a different tunnel capacity and break swap invariance.
Removing late layers changes the classifier interface and degrades accuracy despite saturated intermediate probes.
A single selected split overstates reduced forgetting in shallow networks.
reusable_insights: Profile transfer at every layer before defaulting to the penultimate representation.
Report probe performance and representation dimension/rank together, with fixed tolerance sensitivity.
Distinguish source separability from retention of target-relevant variation.
Treat a proposed depth boundary as a continuum and test several thresholds.
Intervene on rank or delete/freeze layers to separate mechanism from correlation.
Match target-label budget when comparing layer selection and layer fusion.
Condition continual-learning layer claims on task cardinality, similarity, and model capacity.
Use high-resolution many-class and self-supervised models as mandatory external-validity tests.
Validate efficiency recommendations on post-hoc truncation, latency, and accuracy rather than retraining alone.
open_questions: Which objective component causes late rank contraction, and can it be tuned independently of source accuracy?
Does tunnel location predict transfer after controlling for width, layer dimension, and neural-collapse strength?
Can entropy, temperature, or covariance regularization causally preserve target-relevant late features?
Do transformers, language models, and multimodal encoders form one tunnel, repeated tunnels, or none?
Can a boundary be estimated without training a supervised probe at every layer?
When does combining multiple intermediate layers dominate selecting the tunnel entrance?
How stable are tunnel boundaries across seeds, augmentations, optimizers, and label hierarchies?
Can post-hoc layer removal with a small adapter retain source accuracy and improve transfer or forgetting?
How should transferability and OOD detection be balanced when representation collapse helps one and hurts the other?

competitive_landscape.title: Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training
competitive_landscape.difference: Papyan, Han, and Donoho formalize within-class collapse, simplex class means, classifier alignment, and nearest-center decisions near the penultimate layer. The tunnel paper extends the depthwise and transfer view but does not originate class-conditional compression.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Nguyen, Raghu, and Kornblith already find contiguous similar-layer blocks that emerge early and tie them to seed-specific dominant datapoints. The tunnel paper adds rank, transfer, and continual-task consequences and interprets the late block as source-task compression.

competitive_landscape.title: Head2Toe: Utilizing Intermediate Representations for Better Transfer Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Evci et al. select and combine features across all pretrained layers and outperform fine-tuning on OOD VTAB transfer. That is a stronger actionable baseline than selecting one tunnel-entry layer, but it does not diagnose compression or continual forgetting.

competitive_landscape.title: Limitations of Neural Collapse for Understanding Generalization in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Hui, Belkin, and Nakkiran show training collapse need not extend to test data and that terminal training can harm transfer features. The tunnel paper localizes a related transfer decline across depth but still cannot infer generalization from source compression alone.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature learning in deep classifiers through Intermediate Neural Collapse
competitive_landscape.difference: Rangamani et al. analyze covariance and weight/class-mean subspaces across hidden layers, finding progressive intermediate collapse and configuration-dependent failures. The tunnel work adds an explicit probe boundary, OOD transfer curves, and sequential-task swaps.

competitive_landscape.title: What Variables Affect Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Pretrained Models?
competitive_landscape.difference: Harun et al. broaden architectures, resolution, data, and augmentations and conclude that late compression harming transfer is not universal; high-resolution many-class pretraining weakens it. This is the decisive external-validity correction to the reviewed CIFAR/CINIC regime.

competitive_landscape.title: Controlling Neural Collapse Enhances Out-of-Distribution Detection and Transfer Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Harun et al. separate a tradeoff in which stronger collapse aids OOD detection but hurts transfer, then use entropy regularization and fixed simplex projectors at different layers. It turns the tunnel's observational compression link into controllable layerwise objectives.

competitive_landscape.title: Unpacking Softmax: How Temperature Drives Representation Collapse, Compression, and Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Masarczyk et al. identify a softmax-logit-norm rank-deficit bias and manipulate temperature to trade compression against OOD performance across broader models and datasets. It proposes a concrete control variable missing from the tunnel paper's descriptive capacity account.

novelty_assessment: The paper gives a memorable empirical synthesis of late-layer probe saturation, rank contraction, transfer decline, and task-conditioned forgetting under one extractor/tunnel concept. Block-similar layers, intermediate features for transfer, neural collapse, and terminal-training transfer degradation were all established before or concurrently, so the novelty lies in the joint boundary diagnostic and capacity/continual experiments rather than discovering late representation simplification. The class-agnostic and universal wording should be narrowed: unequal tasks break swap invariance, correlation does not identify rank as the cause, and a direct 2024 study finds the transfer-harming tunnel is not universal outside toy-data regimes. Later causal work on collapse control and softmax temperature is a more promising basis for interventions.
